historical_record.description: A charter amendment passed on this day allowed the California Academy of Sciences to build its first building in Golden Gate Park.

The Academy's trustees retained the architect Lewis P. Hobart, who would set the Beaux-Arts plan the buildings followed for four decades. The site chosen was the former location of the Mid-Winter Fair's Mechanical Arts Building.
Work began on North American Hall, called the West Wing, the first building on the Academy's Golden Gate Park site; it was finished in 1916, an early example of a building type then rare in the West.

Steinhart Aquarium opened, the largest and most complete aquarium in the country at the time and one of the first municipal aquariums in the western United States, designed in the Neo-Classical manner by Lewis P. Hobart after he had toured aquariums in Detroit, Washington, Philadelphia, Boston and Miami.

The Academy's East Wing was completed. A rendering of Hobart's proposed north elevation, printed in the San Francisco Chronicle on 25 September 1929, had shown a grand central portico linking the two exhibition halls that was never built.
Simson African Hall was built; the 2003 evaluation found it eligible for the California Register in its own right.
Science Hall was completed to the design of the San Francisco firm Weihe, Frick & Kruse.
Morrison Planetarium, part of Science Hall, was completed — one of the earliest major planetariums in the United States, and found eligible for the California Register in 2003.
Pflueger designed Wattis Hall, a research and exhibition hall of concrete in the Modernist manner, like Cowell Hall before it.
The Fish Roundabout was completed, the first exhibit of its kind in the country.

The City Planning Commission unanimously raised the capital-improvement priority of the California Academy of Sciences' privately funded Hall of Man and Fish Roundabout expansion projects in Golden Gate Park from hold to essential, and found the Academy's projects in conformity with the Master Plan.
The Art Commission approved supplemental Phase 2 plans for Cowell Hall at the Academy of Sciences, by Milton T. Pflueger.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the plans by architect Francis Joseph McCarthy for installing Robert Howard's Whales statue and fountain in the Academy of Sciences courtyard, and took on the planting and care of fifteen sycamores there.
The Recreation and Park Commission moved $3,300 into the 1958 recreation and park bond fund to enlarge the contract of Alek L. Wilson, architect, for the reconstruction of the Steinhart Aquarium.

The Recreation and Park Commission set apart a portion of Golden Gate Park to the California Academy of Sciences for building Cowell Hall, as shown on Milton T. Pflueger's drawing of June 30, subject to the Board of Supervisors' ordinance.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the first phase of John Pflueger's preliminary master plan for the California Academy of Sciences: a new entrance from Middle Drive, a Hall of Anthropology addition with underground parking, and an aquarium addition called the fish roundabout.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the final plans for alterations and improvements to the California Academy of Sciences, whose preliminary plans by John Pflueger it had approved the year before.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the California Academy of Sciences' master plan in its non-peaked-roof version, a three-phase project over six years designed so as to cast no new shadows on the park, with a $2.3 million first phase.

The Board of Park Commissioners approved the plans, presented by Academy director Barton W. Evermann and architect Lewis P. Hobart, for a new wing of the California Academy of Sciences, and let the Academy proceed with its construction.
